title: Saturated, Monounsaturated, and Polyunsaturated Fats: What's the Difference?

seo.title: Saturated vs Monounsaturated vs Polyunsaturated Fat
seo.meta_description: All fats have about 9 calories per gram, but their structures and effects differ. Learn food sources and why replacing saturated fat matters.
seo.search_intent: Understand the major types of dietary fat and choose better sources.

excerpt: Saturated, monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats all provide about 9 calories per gram, but they differ in chemical structure and their effects on blood lipids. The practical question is what replaces what.
content_html:
All dietary fats provide about 9 calories per gram, but they are not metabolically identical. Saturated, monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats are classified by the number of double bonds in their fatty acids.

The three types at a glance

TypeStructureCommon sourcesPractical point
SaturatedNo double bondsButter, full-fat dairy, fatty meat, coconut and palm oilsLimit and replace some with unsaturated fats
MonounsaturatedOne double bondOlive oil, avocado, almonds, peanutsUseful replacement for saturated fat
PolyunsaturatedTwo or more double bondsWalnuts, seeds, soybean/corn oils, fatty fishIncludes essential omega-6 and omega-3 fats

Saturated fat

Saturated fat is common in butter, cream, cheese, fatty cuts of meat and tropical oils. A tablespoon of butter has roughly 7 g saturated fat; a tablespoon of olive oil about 2 g.

Higher saturated-fat intake can raise LDL cholesterol. The replacement matters: swapping saturated fat for unsaturated fat has a different effect than replacing it with refined carbohydrate.

Monounsaturated fat

Oleic acid is the best-known monounsaturated fat and dominates olive oil. It is also abundant in avocado, almonds, peanuts and many other nuts.

One ounce of almonds contains roughly 9 g monounsaturated fat; 100 g avocado about 10 g. Avocado is far less calorie-dense because it contains much more water.

Polyunsaturated fat

This category includes omega-6 and omega-3 families. Linoleic acid (omega-6) and alpha-linolenic acid, or ALA (omega-3), are essential fatty acids that must come from food.

An ounce of walnuts provides roughly 13 g polyunsaturated fat and about 2.6 g ALA. Fatty fish provides EPA and DHA, omega-3s that plant foods do not supply in comparable amounts.

Does saturated fat always look solid?

Many saturated-fat-rich foods are solid at room temperature, but appearance is not a perfect test. Coconut oil can be liquid in a warm room and still contains a very high proportion of saturated fat.

Why replacement matters

Replacing one tablespoon of butter with one tablespoon of olive oil does not dramatically lower calories —both are energy-dense— but it changes the fatty-acid profile substantially.

The American Heart Association recommends replacing foods high in saturated fat with foods containing monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats. Its 2026 guidance continues to emphasize unsaturated-fat sources in place of saturated-fat sources.

What about trans fat?

Trans fat is a separate concern. Industrial partially hydrogenated oils were historically a major source in the U.S. food supply. Trans fats raise cardiovascular risk and should not be grouped with ordinary unsaturated fats just because they contain double bonds.

How much saturated fat?

The American Heart Association recommends aiming for less than 6% of total calories from saturated fat. On a 2,000-calorie diet, that is about 13 g or less per day. Other public-health guidance may use a less restrictive threshold, so individual goals can vary.

Useful substitutions

  • Olive or canola oil instead of butter for many cooking uses.
  • Nuts instead of chips or pastries.
  • Fatty fish instead of a high-saturated-fat meat entrée.
  • Avocado instead of part of a creamy saturated-fat-rich topping.

Bottom line

All fats are calorie-dense, but their health effects differ. A practical eating pattern uses monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats to replace a meaningful share of saturated fat rather than simply adding more fat to the diet.

Sources

Guidance comes from the American Heart Association and FDA.

faq.question: Which is healthier: monounsaturated or polyunsaturated fat?
faq.answer: Both are useful unsaturated fats. Polyunsaturated fats include essential omega-3 and omega-6 fats; monounsaturated fats are abundant in olive oil, avocado and many nuts.

faq.question: Does saturated fat have more calories than unsaturated fat?
faq.answer: No. Both provide about 9 calories per gram.

faq.question: How much saturated fat does the AHA recommend?
faq.answer: The AHA recommends less than 6% of total calories, about 13 g on a 2,000-calorie diet.
